The deadly triad: value estimates that grow on zero reward

Function approximation, bootstrapping and off-policy data each make RL practical. Off-policy value learners such as deep Q-networks (DQN) and soft actor-critic (SAC) use all three, even though together they can let a prediction feed its own target with nothing to pull it back down.

Take a task where every transition gives reward 0, so the true value of every state is 0. You fit a value function from a replay buffer, and the predictions climb anyway: 2, then 4, then past 20, with no reward anywhere to push them up. Where does that value come from? It comes from three habits that every practical value learner wants. Sharing parameters across states lets one update generalize to states you never trained on. Bootstrapping puts the network's own estimate of the next state inside the learning target, so you can learn before an episode ends. Off-policy learning lets you reuse experience that some other policy collected. Sutton and Barto call the combination the deadly triad. What I like about it is that the failure needs nothing exotic. It only needs a feedback loop small enough to fit on one blackboard.

Let's build the smallest one, a construction from Tsitsiklis and Van Roy (as presented by van Hasselt et al., §2). There are two states, s₁ and s₂. Our little network has one knob, w: it predicts w at s₁ and twice that at s₂. The policy we want to evaluate goes from s₁ to s₂ and then stays at s₂ forever, but the replay buffer holds only that first step. Let's do one update. With w = 1 we predict 1 at s₁, but the target is 0 + 0.9 × 2 = 1.8 (0.9 is the discount). Moving 10% of the way toward that target raises w to 1.08. Seems reasonable! Except we also just raised the prediction at s₂ to 2.16, so the next target is higher too. The board shows how this feeds on itself.

The columns at the bottom of the board change one ingredient each, and each change interrupts this example's feedback. A general convergence guarantee takes more assumptions (I've put those in the notes below). The linear one covers a fixed policy with linear features, so it says nothing about neural networks or a policy that keeps changing. Okay, so do the algorithms we actually use contain all three ingredients? DQN and SAC do. They lean on replay, which breaks up correlated samples, and on slowly refreshed target weights, which slow the loop down. Neither one closes the loop: in our example, every target copy still multiplies w by more than 1.

If your own estimates climb, first compare them with the discounted-return cap on the board, using your task's reward scale. Mask terminal steps before you trust that check, or future value leaks past the end of an episode. A modest overshoot is ordinary estimation error, and a policy can perform well while its values are wrong. When estimates keep climbing, trace the loop. Which states and actions never get updated? How far does one update move other predictions? How often does the target refresh? Where does the gradient stop? In our example, fitting s₁ raised the prediction at s₂, that raised the next target, and the buffer never gave us an s₂ update to correct it. That's the loop I'd look for in a run whose values keep growing.

Exact conditions and sources
  • On-policy linear TD (Tsitsiklis and Van Roy, §§IV, VII): fixed policy; finite, irreducible, aperiodic chain visited on-policy; bounded rewards; 0 ≤ γ < 1; fixed, linearly independent features; positive step sizes with Σαt = ∞ and Σαt² < ∞. Under these conditions, the projected Bellman operator is a γ-contraction in the norm weighted by the visit distribution, with a unique projected fixed point. The two-state chain is not irreducible and its column uses a constant step, so the column shows only the correcting update.
  • Fixed labels (Sutton and Barto, §§5.5, 9.2): in general the labels come from finished episodes. Each label is ρG, where G is the discounted reward sum to the end of the episode and ρ is the product of π/b over the rest of the episode. The two-state example never ends, so its column supplies the known return 0 directly. With full-rank features and 0 < η < 2/λmax(XᵀX), gradient descent reaches the unique least-squares fit of the recorded data. Whether that fit matches the true target-policy values is a separate statistical question. It needs behavior support for the target's actions and finite label variance, and large importance weights make it worse.
  • Tabular Q-learning (Watkins and Dayan, 1992; see the Q-learning tree): finite MDP with stationary rewards and transitions, bounded rewards, γ < 1, every state-action pair updated infinitely often, per-pair steps in [0, 1) with an infinite sum and a finite sum of squares. The max-norm contraction ‖T*q − T*u‖∞ ≤ γ‖q − u‖∞ gives one fixed point: the optimal table.
  • Methods: DQN (Mnih et al., 2015) used minibatches of 32, RMSProp and error clipping to [−1, 1]. Its target is r + γ(1 − d) max Qθ⁻(s′, a′), where d masks terminal steps. SAC (2018) also takes the minimum of two Q-functions. The PPO (2017) critic uses λ = 0.95 λ-returns in the Baselines implementation. GRPO (DeepSeekMath, 2024) dropped the value model to save memory, and because per-token values are hard to learn when the reward arrives at the final token. RLOO compares several sampled answers for the same prompt. RECAP (π*0.6, 2025) uses a learned value 50 steps ahead inside the policy's advantage, but it does not bootstrap the value network itself. See reward-aware learning from fixed data.
